passages.title: Two sons seek David's throne
passages.summary: King David is old and weak. His son Adonijah declares himself king with the support of Joab and the priest Abiathar. He holds a feast and leaves out Solomon and the prophet Nathan. Nathan sends Bathsheba to remind David of his oath about Solomon. Nathan follows her in and confirms her report. David orders Solomon to ride the royal mule to Gihon. Zadok the priest anoints him, and the city shouts. Adonijah’s guests scatter, and he begs Solomon for his life.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Who speaks for Solomon when David must choose the next king?

contextNote.title: Succession requires a decision before the king dies
contextNote.text: Verse 6 says David never questioned Adonijah about his conduct. Verse 18 says the king does not know what is happening. Bathsheba’s words in verse 20 put the decision where it belongs. All Israel is waiting for David to name his heir. She also names the danger to herself and her son (verse 21). Nathan arranges for two voices to bring the same report (verses 13–14). The oath she cites is not recorded earlier in these books.

passages.title: David dies and Solomon consolidates power
passages.summary: David tells Solomon to keep the LORD’s law and to deal with Joab and Shimei. David dies after forty years as king. Adonijah asks Bathsheba to request David’s last attendant, Abishag, as his wife. Solomon reads this as a claim to the throne and has him killed. He sends the priest Abiathar home to Anathoth. Joab flees to the altar and is killed there. Shimei is confined to Jerusalem and dies when he leaves it. The kingdom is now firmly in Solomon’s hand.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: How does Solomon explain his orders against each rival?

contextNote.title: The new throne is secured through removals
contextNote.text: Each removal in this chapter comes with a stated reason. Adonijah asked for a woman of the late king’s household (verse 22). Joab had killed two commanders in peacetime (verse 32). Shimei broke his sworn terms (verse 43). In verse 26 Abiathar is spared for his years of loyalty to David. Verse 27 links his removal to the word against Eli’s house. The reader sees justice and advantage served by the same acts.

passages.title: Solomon asks for wisdom and judges a dispute
passages.summary: Solomon marries Pharaoh’s daughter and brings her to Jerusalem. He offers sacrifices at Gibeon, and the LORD appears to him in a dream. God tells him to ask for what he wants. Solomon asks for an understanding heart to judge the people. God is pleased and adds riches and honor. Two prostitutes then come to him, each claiming the same living baby. Solomon calls for a sword to divide the child. The true mother gives up her claim, and he returns the child to her.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me encourages seeking discernment between right and wrong. What does Solomon ask for in verse 9, and for whose benefit?

contextNote.title: Wisdom begins as a request to hear people well
contextNote.text: Solomon calls himself “a little child” in verse 7. His request in verse 9 is for a heart that hears. He wants it in order to judge God’s people, not for himself. Verse 11 lists what he did not ask for: long life, riches, his enemies’ deaths. The first case tests the gift. Two women of low standing come with no witnesses (verse 18). The king hears them and finds the one who loves the child.

passages.title: Officials, provisions, and wisdom
passages.summary: The chapter lists Solomon’s chief officials. Twelve officers govern twelve districts. Each district supplies the king’s household for one month of the year. Judah and Israel are as many as the sand, eating and drinking. The court uses huge amounts of flour, meal, and meat each day. Everyone lives safely under his own vine and fig tree. God gives Solomon wisdom beyond all the people of the East. He speaks three thousand proverbs and teaches about trees and animals.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Who provides the food that supports Solomon’s court?

contextNote.title: Royal abundance requires a system of supply
contextNote.text: Verses 22–23 give the court’s food for a single day. Verse 27 says where it came from. Twelve officers collected it, each for one month (verse 7). The chapter also shows general plenty and safety (verses 20 and 25). Both pictures stand together. Samuel warned that a king would “take” fields and produce (1 Samuel 8:14–15). In 12:4 the people call Solomon’s rule a heavy yoke.

passages.title: Hiram supplies timber for the temple
passages.summary: King Hiram of Tyre sends greetings to Solomon. Solomon says he will build a house for the LORD’s name. He asks for cedar from Lebanon, cut by skilled Sidonians. Hiram agrees and floats the logs down the coast. Solomon pays him each year in wheat and oil. The two kings make a treaty. Solomon drafts thirty thousand Israelites to work in Lebanon in shifts. Thousands more carry loads and cut great stones for the foundation.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: What does temple building require from the workers and their families?

contextNote.title: The building's beauty depends on counted labor
contextNote.text: The temple begins with a trade deal and a labor draft. Verse 13 says the draft came “out of all Israel.” Each man spends one month in Lebanon and two at home (verse 14). Verses 15–16 count the carriers, stonecutters, and overseers. Adoniram, who runs the draft, is stoned in 12:18. Chapter 9:22 says Solomon made no Israelite a bondservant. The book keeps both statements.

passages.title: The temple is built
passages.summary: Solomon begins the temple in the fourth year of his reign. The house is sixty cubits long, twenty wide, and thirty high. Its stones are finished at the quarry, so no iron tool is heard on site. The LORD tells Solomon the promise holds if he keeps the commandments. The inside is lined with cedar and covered with gold. Two gold-covered cherubim stand in the inner room. The walls and doors are carved with palms and flowers. The work takes seven years.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me invites reflection on sacred space and temple symbols. What condition does verse 12 attach to the building?

contextNote.title: A building cannot replace the duties attached to it
contextNote.text: The chapter is almost all measurements and materials. Verses 11–13 interrupt it with a message. Verse 12 begins with “if” and names statutes, ordinances, and commandments. The promise to David depends on the king’s conduct. Verse 13 says the LORD will dwell “among the children of Israel.” It does not say he will live in the building. Chapter 9:6–7 states what happens to the house if the condition fails.

passages.title: Royal buildings and bronze furnishings
passages.summary: Solomon spends thirteen years building his own palace. It includes the House of the Forest of Lebanon and a hall for judging. He builds a similar house for Pharaoh’s daughter. He brings Hiram, a bronze worker, from Tyre. Hiram casts two great pillars named Jachin and Boaz. He makes a huge basin called the sea, set on twelve bronze oxen. He makes ten wheeled stands, basins, pots, and shovels. Solomon adds the gold furnishings and David’s dedicated treasures.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older Church manual compares the bronze sea with baptism. What does verse 14 say about the craftsman’s family and skill?

contextNote.title: A temple depends on skilled workers
contextNote.text: Verse 14 introduces the craftsman by his parents. His mother was an Israelite widow, and his father a man of Tyre. The verse says he was filled with wisdom, understanding, and skill. Exodus 31:3 uses the same three terms for Bezalel, who built the tabernacle. So the text counts a metalworker’s skill as a kind of wisdom. A man of two peoples makes the temple’s bronze. The bronze stand shown is a regional comparison, not a temple vessel.

passages.title: The ark enters the temple and Solomon prays
passages.summary: The elders and priests bring the ark into the temple. A cloud fills the house, and the priests cannot stand to serve. Solomon blesses the people and prays before the altar. He says heaven itself cannot contain God, much less this house. He asks God to hear prayers made toward it. He names drought, famine, defeat, and exile as times to pray. He asks God to hear the foreigner too. Israel then offers sacrifices and keeps a feast for fourteen days.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects the dedication prayer with temple covenants and walking in God’s ways. Whom does Solomon pray for in verses 41–43?

contextNote.title: The dedication imagines listeners beyond Israel
contextNote.text: Solomon’s prayer lists seven kinds of need. The fifth, in verses 41–43, concerns a person outside Israel. That foreigner has heard of God’s name and comes from far away. Solomon asks God to do all the foreigner requests. The stated aim is that all peoples may know God’s name (verse 43). Verse 27 has already said no house can contain God. Verses 46–50 even expect a day when Israel prays from exile.

passages.title: Promises, warnings, labor, and trade
passages.summary: The LORD appears to Solomon a second time and accepts the temple. If Solomon walks as David did, his throne will last. If Israel turns to other gods, the land and the house will be lost. Solomon gives Hiram twenty towns in Galilee, and Hiram is not pleased. Solomon uses forced labor to build Jerusalem’s wall, Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer. The remaining Canaanite peoples are made laborers. Israelites serve as soldiers and officers. Solomon builds ships on the Red Sea that bring gold from Ophir.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies God’s promises and the responsibility to keep covenants. What does verse 7 say could happen to the temple?

contextNote.title: The warning imagines the temple as a future ruin
contextNote.text: This answer comes just after the temple’s dedication. Verse 3 says God has made the house holy. Verse 7 says that same house can be cast out of his sight. Its holiness comes from God and depends on Israel’s loyalty. Verses 8–9 picture people passing the ruin and asking why. The answer given is that Israel left the LORD for other gods. Second Kings 25:9 reports the day the house was burned.

passages.title: The queen of Sheba visits
passages.summary: The queen of Sheba hears of Solomon and comes to test him with hard questions. He answers them all. She sees his house, his table, his servants, and his offerings. She says the report she heard was not even half the truth. She blesses the LORD, who made him king to do justice. They exchange rich gifts, and she goes home. Solomon’s yearly gold, his ivory throne, and his golden cups are described. He gathers chariots and buys horses from Egypt.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: What impresses the queen besides Solomon’s wealth?

contextNote.title: A visitor's praise presents one view of courtly success
contextNote.text: The queen judges the court by what a visitor can see. In verse 8 she calls the servants happy because they hear his wisdom. In verse 9 she states what a king is for: justice and righteousness. The rest of the chapter counts gold, shields, and horses (verses 14–29). Deuteronomy 17:16–17 told kings not to pile up horses, wives, or gold. It names Egypt as the source of horses. The chapter makes no comment, and chapter 11 does.

passages.title: Solomon turns away and adversaries rise
passages.summary: Solomon loves many foreign women and has a thousand wives and concubines. In his old age they turn his heart to other gods. He builds high places for the gods of Moab and Ammon. The LORD says the kingdom will be torn from his son. One tribe will remain for David’s sake. Enemies rise in Edom and Damascus. The prophet Ahijah tears a new cloak and gives ten pieces to an officer, Jeroboam. Solomon tries to kill Jeroboam, who flees to Egypt until Solomon dies.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks readers to examine influences that turn their hearts from God. What does Ahijah do with the garment in verse 30?

contextNote.title: A divided garment makes a political warning visible
contextNote.text: Ahijah acts out his message before he speaks it. The cloak is new, and he tears it into twelve pieces (verse 30). Ten go to Jeroboam, and one tribe stays with David’s house (verses 31–32). The text does not explain the missing piece. A torn robe also marked Saul’s loss of the kingdom (1 Samuel 15:27–28). The reason given is worship of other gods (verse 33). Jeroboam receives a promise with a condition, as David’s house did (verse 38).

passages.title: Rehoboam rejects the petition and the kingdom divides
passages.summary: Rehoboam goes to Shechem to be made king. Jeroboam and the people ask him to lighten Solomon’s heavy labor. The old advisers tell him to serve the people and speak kindly. The young men tell him to promise a heavier yoke. He follows the young men and threatens scorpions for whips. Ten tribes reject David’s house and make Jeroboam king. A prophet stops Rehoboam from going to war. Jeroboam sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan to keep his people from Jerusalem.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the effect of leaders’ choices and the need for good counsel. What do the people offer Rehoboam in verse 4?

contextNote.title: The divided kingdom begins with a labor complaint
contextNote.text: The people’s request in verse 4 is an offer, not a revolt. They will serve the new king if he eases the labor. The elders see that the king must first serve them (verse 7). Rehoboam chooses the harsh answer in verse 14. Verse 15 adds that the turn of events came from the LORD. The text names both the king’s folly and God’s purpose. The cry in verse 16 repeats Sheba’s words from 2 Samuel 20:1.

passages.title: A man of God confronts Bethel
passages.summary: A man of God from Judah cries out against Jeroboam’s altar at Bethel. The altar splits, and the king’s hand withers and is healed. The man refuses the king’s meal, as God commanded him. An old prophet of Bethel rides after him. The old man lies and says an angel told him to bring the visitor home. The man of God eats, and a word comes that he will die. A lion kills him on the road and stands beside the body. The old prophet buries him in his own tomb.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Why does the visiting prophet accept a claim that changes his earlier command?

contextNote.title: An authoritative claim can still deceive
contextNote.text: The man of God turned down a king’s reward without trouble (verses 8–9). He gives way to a fellow prophet. His own command came to him directly (verse 9). The new one comes secondhand, and it reverses the first. Verse 18 says plainly, “He lied to him,” and gives no motive. Strangely, the liar then speaks a true word (verses 20–22). The lion kills but does not eat, which marks a sign (verse 28).

passages.title: Ahijah speaks and Shishak attacks Jerusalem
passages.summary: Jeroboam’s son falls sick. He sends his wife in disguise to the prophet Ahijah at Shiloh. Ahijah is blind, but the LORD tells him who is coming. He says Jeroboam’s whole house will be cut off for its idols. The child will die when she reaches home. Israel itself will be uprooted and scattered. In Judah, Rehoboam’s people build high places and sacred pillars. Shishak king of Egypt takes the temple’s treasures and Solomon’s gold shields.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: How does Ahijah’s message affect Jeroboam’s wife and child?

contextNote.title: Disguise cannot control the answer sought
contextNote.text: Jeroboam sends to the prophet who once promised him a kingdom (verse 2). He hides who is asking. The disguise is useless twice: Ahijah is blind and has been told (verses 4–5). Verse 6 greets her by name at the door. She came for a word about one child and hears about a whole house. The boy dies as her feet cross the threshold (verse 17). Verse 13 calls his burial a kindness, since something good was found in him.

passages.title: Judah’s rulers and a new northern dynasty
passages.summary: Abijam rules Judah three years and follows his father’s sins. For David’s sake the LORD keeps a lamp in Jerusalem. Asa rules forty-one years and does what is right. He removes idols and even deposes his grandmother for her idol. Baasha of Israel fortifies Ramah to block Judah. Asa sends temple and palace treasure to Ben Hadad of Syria. Ben Hadad attacks northern Israel, and Baasha withdraws. In Israel, Baasha has killed Nadab and all Jeroboam’s house.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: What does Asa give away to gain help against Baasha?

contextNote.title: An alliance purchases relief by changing another ruler's loyalties
contextNote.text: Asa is one of the kings this book praises (verses 11–14). His answer to a border threat is to buy a foreign army. The payment in verse 18 comes from the temple’s own treasure. Verse 19 asks Ben Hadad to break his treaty with Israel. The plan works (verses 20–22). The price is paid by Israelite towns in the north. Second Chronicles 16:7–9 records a prophet’s rebuke for this bargain.

passages.title: Kings fall before Omri and Ahab rise
passages.summary: A prophet tells Baasha that his house will end like Jeroboam’s. His son Elah is killed while drunk by Zimri, a chariot commander. Zimri rules seven days and burns the palace over himself. Omri defeats a rival and becomes king. He buys the hill of Samaria and builds his capital there. His son Ahab marries Jezebel of Sidon and builds a temple for Baal. Ahab does more evil than all before him. In his days a man rebuilds Jericho at the cost of two sons.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: How do the changes of kings affect their families and towns?

contextNote.title: A new capital survives rapid changes of rulers
contextNote.text: This chapter moves through five rulers in thirty-four verses. Three of them die by violence or fire. Verse 24 records the one act of Omri that lasts. He buys a hill at a fair price and names the city for its seller. Samaria remains the capital until the kingdom falls (2 Kings 17:5–6). The book judges Omri only by his worship (verses 25–26). Verse 34 ties Jericho’s rebuilding to Joshua’s curse (Joshua 6:26).

passages.title: Elijah and the widow at Zarephath
passages.summary: Elijah tells Ahab there will be no dew or rain except at his word. The LORD hides him by a brook, where ravens bring him food. The brook dries up. The LORD sends him to a widow in Zarephath, a town of Sidon. She is gathering sticks to cook a last meal for herself and her son. Elijah asks for a small cake first and promises the flour and oil will last. They do. Later her son dies, Elijah prays, and the boy lives again.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the widow’s trust amid scarcity. What does the widow have left in verse 12?

contextNote.title: A prophet depends on a household already facing hunger
contextNote.text: Zarephath belongs to Sidon (verse 9), the homeland of Jezebel (16:31). The prophet is sent outside Israel to be fed. His host is a widow with one handful of meal (verse 12). She speaks of “the LORD your God,” not her own. Elijah asks her to feed him first and gives a promise (verses 13–14). Verse 15 says she went and did it. Jesus later cites her in Luke 4:25–26.

passages.title: Elijah confronts Ahab at Carmel
passages.summary: In the third year of drought the LORD sends Elijah to Ahab. Ahab’s steward Obadiah has hidden a hundred prophets from Jezebel. Elijah gathers Israel and four hundred fifty prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel. Each side prepares a bull, and the God who answers by fire is God. Baal’s prophets cry out all day, and nothing happens. Elijah rebuilds the LORD’s altar and drenches it with water. He prays, and fire falls and burns up everything. The people confess the LORD, Baal’s prophets are killed, and rain comes.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me uses Elijah’s challenge to examine commitment to God. How do the people answer Elijah’s question in verse 21?

contextNote.title: A public question frames the contest as a choice
contextNote.text: Elijah’s question in verse 21 allows no middle position. The people say nothing, since they have been keeping both. He then sets terms that favor the other side. Baal’s prophets are many, go first, and have most of the day (verses 22–29). Elijah soaks his own offering three times (verses 33–35). His prayer is short and asks that the people may know (verses 36–37). In verse 39 the silent crowd finally answers.

passages.title: Elijah receives care and calls Elisha
passages.summary: Jezebel swears to kill Elijah, and he runs for his life. In the wilderness he sits under a tree and asks to die. An angel twice wakes him and gives him food and water. He travels forty days to Horeb, the mountain of God. There a wind, an earthquake, and a fire pass, and then a quiet voice. Elijah says he alone is left. The LORD sends him to anoint two kings and Elisha. Elisha leaves his oxen and follows him.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate regions. Disputed sites and exact buildings remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the quiet voice and Elisha’s willingness to respond. How many does the LORD say remain faithful in verse 18?

contextNote.title: Elijah's isolation differs from the larger situation described
contextNote.text: Elijah says twice that he alone is left (verses 10 and 14). The quiet voice between them does not change his words. The LORD’s first answer to his despair was food and sleep (verses 5–7). The second is work: three people to anoint (verses 15–16). Verse 18 then corrects his count with seven thousand. Obadiah’s hundred prophets were also still alive (18:13). In Elisha he is given a successor.

passages.title: Ahab defeats Ben Hadad and releases him
passages.summary: Ben Hadad of Syria besieges Samaria and demands Ahab’s treasure and family. A prophet promises Ahab victory, and Israel wins. The Syrians decide the LORD is a god of the hills only. They return in spring and lose again on the plain. Ben Hadad’s servants come in sackcloth to beg for his life. Ahab calls him “my brother” and makes a treaty. A prophet in disguise tells Ahab a story and condemns him with it. Ahab goes home sullen and angry.

contextNote.title: A victorious treaty receives a different prophetic judgment
contextNote.text: A prophet said the victory was given so Israel would know the LORD (verse 28). Ahab treats it as a chance for trade. Verse 34 lists his gains: towns returned and markets in Damascus. He frees the king on those terms. The prophet’s staged case works as Nathan’s story did (verses 39–40). Ahab passes sentence on himself. Verse 42 says the man he released was not his to release.

passages.title: Naboth is killed and Elijah confronts Ahab
passages.summary: Naboth owns a vineyard beside Ahab’s palace in Jezreel. Ahab offers him money or a better vineyard, and Naboth refuses. Ahab lies on his bed and will not eat. Jezebel writes letters in his name to the town’s elders. Two false witnesses accuse Naboth of cursing God and the king. He is stoned, and Ahab goes down to take the vineyard. Elijah meets him there with the LORD’s sentence on his house. Ahab humbles himself, and the disaster is delayed to his son’s time.

lds.text: How do Ahab and Jezebel use their power against Naboth? What does Elijah say about their actions?

contextNote.title: An inherited field is more than a commodity
contextNote.text: Ahab’s offer in verse 2 is fair as a sale. Naboth’s refusal in verse 3 rests on something else. The field is his fathers’ inheritance, and he calls on the LORD. Leviticus 25:23 and Numbers 36:7 keep such land within the family. Ahab sulks (verse 4), and Jezebel asks whether he rules Israel (verse 7). The tablet shows an ordinary field sale, the kind Naboth refuses. She then uses Israel’s own court forms, with two witnesses, to kill (verses 9–10).

passages.title: Micaiah warns Ahab before the final battle
passages.summary: Jehoshaphat of Judah visits Ahab, who wants to retake Ramoth Gilead. Four hundred prophets promise success. Jehoshaphat asks for one more, and Ahab names Micaiah, whom he hates. Micaiah sees Israel scattered like sheep without a shepherd. He describes a lying spirit sent into the mouths of Ahab’s prophets. Ahab jails him and goes to battle in disguise. A random arrow strikes Ahab between the plates of his armor. He dies at evening, and dogs lick his blood in Samaria.

contextNote.title: The court pressures a speaker to match an approved answer
contextNote.text: The messenger in verse 13 means well. He asks Micaiah to agree with the four hundred. Micaiah answers that he will say what the LORD says (verse 14). Ahab himself knows the first cheerful answer is false (verse 16). He demands the truth and has already said he hates it (verse 8). He jails the man who gives it (verse 27). The disguise fails against an arrow shot “at random” (verse 34).

events.title: Two sons seek David's throne
events.summary: King David is old and weak. His son Adonijah declares himself king with the support of Joab and the priest Abiathar. He holds a feast and leaves out Solomon and the prophet Nathan. Nathan sends Bathsheba to remind David of his oath about Solomon. Nathan follows her in and confirms her report. David orders Solomon to ride the royal mule to Gihon. Zadok the priest anoints him, and the city shouts. Adonijah’s guests scatter, and he begs Solomon for his life.
events.detail: Verse 6 says David never questioned Adonijah about his conduct. Verse 18 says the king does not know what is happening. Bathsheba’s words in verse 20 put the decision where it belongs. All Israel is waiting for David to name his heir. She also names the danger to herself and her son (verse 21). Nathan arranges for two voices to bring the same report (verses 13–14). The oath she cites is not recorded earlier in these books.

events.title: David dies and Solomon consolidates power
events.summary: David tells Solomon to keep the LORD’s law and to deal with Joab and Shimei. David dies after forty years as king. Adonijah asks Bathsheba to request David’s last attendant, Abishag, as his wife. Solomon reads this as a claim to the throne and has him killed. He sends the priest Abiathar home to Anathoth. Joab flees to the altar and is killed there. Shimei is confined to Jerusalem and dies when he leaves it. The kingdom is now firmly in Solomon’s hand.
events.detail: Each removal in this chapter comes with a stated reason. Adonijah asked for a woman of the late king’s household (verse 22). Joab had killed two commanders in peacetime (verse 32). Shimei broke his sworn terms (verse 43). In verse 26 Abiathar is spared for his years of loyalty to David. Verse 27 links his removal to the word against Eli’s house. The reader sees justice and advantage served by the same acts.

events.title: Solomon asks for wisdom and judges a dispute
events.summary: Solomon marries Pharaoh’s daughter and brings her to Jerusalem. He offers sacrifices at Gibeon, and the LORD appears to him in a dream. God tells him to ask for what he wants. Solomon asks for an understanding heart to judge the people. God is pleased and adds riches and honor. Two prostitutes then come to him, each claiming the same living baby. Solomon calls for a sword to divide the child. The true mother gives up her claim, and he returns the child to her.
events.detail: Solomon calls himself “a little child” in verse 7. His request in verse 9 is for a heart that hears. He wants it in order to judge God’s people, not for himself. Verse 11 lists what he did not ask for: long life, riches, his enemies’ deaths. The first case tests the gift. Two women of low standing come with no witnesses (verse 18). The king hears them and finds the one who loves the child.

events.title: Officials, provisions, and wisdom
events.summary: The chapter lists Solomon’s chief officials. Twelve officers govern twelve districts. Each district supplies the king’s household for one month of the year. Judah and Israel are as many as the sand, eating and drinking. The court uses huge amounts of flour, meal, and meat each day. Everyone lives safely under his own vine and fig tree. God gives Solomon wisdom beyond all the people of the East. He speaks three thousand proverbs and teaches about trees and animals.
events.detail: Verses 22–23 give the court’s food for a single day. Verse 27 says where it came from. Twelve officers collected it, each for one month (verse 7). The chapter also shows general plenty and safety (verses 20 and 25). Both pictures stand together. Samuel warned that a king would “take” fields and produce (1 Samuel 8:14–15). In 12:4 the people call Solomon’s rule a heavy yoke.

events.title: Hiram supplies timber for the temple
events.summary: King Hiram of Tyre sends greetings to Solomon. Solomon says he will build a house for the LORD’s name. He asks for cedar from Lebanon, cut by skilled Sidonians. Hiram agrees and floats the logs down the coast. Solomon pays him each year in wheat and oil. The two kings make a treaty. Solomon drafts thirty thousand Israelites to work in Lebanon in shifts. Thousands more carry loads and cut great stones for the foundation.
events.detail: The temple begins with a trade deal and a labor draft. Verse 13 says the draft came “out of all Israel.” Each man spends one month in Lebanon and two at home (verse 14). Verses 15–16 count the carriers, stonecutters, and overseers. Adoniram, who runs the draft, is stoned in 12:18. Chapter 9:22 says Solomon made no Israelite a bondservant. The book keeps both statements.

events.title: The temple is built
events.summary: Solomon begins the temple in the fourth year of his reign. The house is sixty cubits long, twenty wide, and thirty high. Its stones are finished at the quarry, so no iron tool is heard on site. The LORD tells Solomon the promise holds if he keeps the commandments. The inside is lined with cedar and covered with gold. Two gold-covered cherubim stand in the inner room. The walls and doors are carved with palms and flowers. The work takes seven years.
events.detail: The chapter is almost all measurements and materials. Verses 11–13 interrupt it with a message. Verse 12 begins with “if” and names statutes, ordinances, and commandments. The promise to David depends on the king’s conduct. Verse 13 says the LORD will dwell “among the children of Israel.” It does not say he will live in the building. Chapter 9:6–7 states what happens to the house if the condition fails.

events.title: Royal buildings and bronze furnishings
events.summary: Solomon spends thirteen years building his own palace. It includes the House of the Forest of Lebanon and a hall for judging. He builds a similar house for Pharaoh’s daughter. He brings Hiram, a bronze worker, from Tyre. Hiram casts two great pillars named Jachin and Boaz. He makes a huge basin called the sea, set on twelve bronze oxen. He makes ten wheeled stands, basins, pots, and shovels. Solomon adds the gold furnishings and David’s dedicated treasures.
events.detail: Verse 14 introduces the craftsman by his parents. His mother was an Israelite widow, and his father a man of Tyre. The verse says he was filled with wisdom, understanding, and skill. Exodus 31:3 uses the same three terms for Bezalel, who built the tabernacle. So the text counts a metalworker’s skill as a kind of wisdom. A man of two peoples makes the temple’s bronze. The bronze stand shown is a regional comparison, not a temple vessel.

events.title: The ark enters the temple and Solomon prays
events.summary: The elders and priests bring the ark into the temple. A cloud fills the house, and the priests cannot stand to serve. Solomon blesses the people and prays before the altar. He says heaven itself cannot contain God, much less this house. He asks God to hear prayers made toward it. He names drought, famine, defeat, and exile as times to pray. He asks God to hear the foreigner too. Israel then offers sacrifices and keeps a feast for fourteen days.
events.detail: Solomon’s prayer lists seven kinds of need. The fifth, in verses 41–43, concerns a person outside Israel. That foreigner has heard of God’s name and comes from far away. Solomon asks God to do all the foreigner requests. The stated aim is that all peoples may know God’s name (verse 43). Verse 27 has already said no house can contain God. Verses 46–50 even expect a day when Israel prays from exile.

events.title: Promises, warnings, labor, and trade
events.summary: The LORD appears to Solomon a second time and accepts the temple. If Solomon walks as David did, his throne will last. If Israel turns to other gods, the land and the house will be lost. Solomon gives Hiram twenty towns in Galilee, and Hiram is not pleased. Solomon uses forced labor to build Jerusalem’s wall, Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer. The remaining Canaanite peoples are made laborers. Israelites serve as soldiers and officers. Solomon builds ships on the Red Sea that bring gold from Ophir.
events.detail: This answer comes just after the temple’s dedication. Verse 3 says God has made the house holy. Verse 7 says that same house can be cast out of his sight. Its holiness comes from God and depends on Israel’s loyalty. Verses 8–9 picture people passing the ruin and asking why. The answer given is that Israel left the LORD for other gods. Second Kings 25:9 reports the day the house was burned.

events.title: The queen of Sheba visits
events.summary: The queen of Sheba hears of Solomon and comes to test him with hard questions. He answers them all. She sees his house, his table, his servants, and his offerings. She says the report she heard was not even half the truth. She blesses the LORD, who made him king to do justice. They exchange rich gifts, and she goes home. Solomon’s yearly gold, his ivory throne, and his golden cups are described. He gathers chariots and buys horses from Egypt.
events.detail: The queen judges the court by what a visitor can see. In verse 8 she calls the servants happy because they hear his wisdom. In verse 9 she states what a king is for: justice and righteousness. The rest of the chapter counts gold, shields, and horses (verses 14–29). Deuteronomy 17:16–17 told kings not to pile up horses, wives, or gold. It names Egypt as the source of horses. The chapter makes no comment, and chapter 11 does.

events.title: Solomon turns away and adversaries rise
events.summary: Solomon loves many foreign women and has a thousand wives and concubines. In his old age they turn his heart to other gods. He builds high places for the gods of Moab and Ammon. The LORD says the kingdom will be torn from his son. One tribe will remain for David’s sake. Enemies rise in Edom and Damascus. The prophet Ahijah tears a new cloak and gives ten pieces to an officer, Jeroboam. Solomon tries to kill Jeroboam, who flees to Egypt until Solomon dies.
events.detail: Ahijah acts out his message before he speaks it. The cloak is new, and he tears it into twelve pieces (verse 30). Ten go to Jeroboam, and one tribe stays with David’s house (verses 31–32). The text does not explain the missing piece. A torn robe also marked Saul’s loss of the kingdom (1 Samuel 15:27–28). The reason given is worship of other gods (verse 33). Jeroboam receives a promise with a condition, as David’s house did (verse 38).

events.title: Rehoboam rejects the petition and the kingdom divides
events.summary: Rehoboam goes to Shechem to be made king. Jeroboam and the people ask him to lighten Solomon’s heavy labor. The old advisers tell him to serve the people and speak kindly. The young men tell him to promise a heavier yoke. He follows the young men and threatens scorpions for whips. Ten tribes reject David’s house and make Jeroboam king. A prophet stops Rehoboam from going to war. Jeroboam sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan to keep his people from Jerusalem.
events.detail: The people’s request in verse 4 is an offer, not a revolt. They will serve the new king if he eases the labor. The elders see that the king must first serve them (verse 7). Rehoboam chooses the harsh answer in verse 14. Verse 15 adds that the turn of events came from the LORD. The text names both the king’s folly and God’s purpose. The cry in verse 16 repeats Sheba’s words from 2 Samuel 20:1.

events.title: A man of God confronts Bethel
events.summary: A man of God from Judah cries out against Jeroboam’s altar at Bethel. The altar splits, and the king’s hand withers and is healed. The man refuses the king’s meal, as God commanded him. An old prophet of Bethel rides after him. The old man lies and says an angel told him to bring the visitor home. The man of God eats, and a word comes that he will die. A lion kills him on the road and stands beside the body. The old prophet buries him in his own tomb.
events.detail: The man of God turned down a king’s reward without trouble (verses 8–9). He gives way to a fellow prophet. His own command came to him directly (verse 9). The new one comes secondhand, and it reverses the first. Verse 18 says plainly, “He lied to him,” and gives no motive. Strangely, the liar then speaks a true word (verses 20–22). The lion kills but does not eat, which marks a sign (verse 28).

events.title: Ahijah speaks and Shishak attacks Jerusalem
events.summary: Jeroboam’s son falls sick. He sends his wife in disguise to the prophet Ahijah at Shiloh. Ahijah is blind, but the LORD tells him who is coming. He says Jeroboam’s whole house will be cut off for its idols. The child will die when she reaches home. Israel itself will be uprooted and scattered. In Judah, Rehoboam’s people build high places and sacred pillars. Shishak king of Egypt takes the temple’s treasures and Solomon’s gold shields.
events.detail: Jeroboam sends to the prophet who once promised him a kingdom (verse 2). He hides who is asking. The disguise is useless twice: Ahijah is blind and has been told (verses 4–5). Verse 6 greets her by name at the door. She came for a word about one child and hears about a whole house. The boy dies as her feet cross the threshold (verse 17). Verse 13 calls his burial a kindness, since something good was found in him.

events.title: Judah’s rulers and a new northern dynasty
events.summary: Abijam rules Judah three years and follows his father’s sins. For David’s sake the LORD keeps a lamp in Jerusalem. Asa rules forty-one years and does what is right. He removes idols and even deposes his grandmother for her idol. Baasha of Israel fortifies Ramah to block Judah. Asa sends temple and palace treasure to Ben Hadad of Syria. Ben Hadad attacks northern Israel, and Baasha withdraws. In Israel, Baasha has killed Nadab and all Jeroboam’s house.
events.detail: Asa is one of the kings this book praises (verses 11–14). His answer to a border threat is to buy a foreign army. The payment in verse 18 comes from the temple’s own treasure. Verse 19 asks Ben Hadad to break his treaty with Israel. The plan works (verses 20–22). The price is paid by Israelite towns in the north. Second Chronicles 16:7–9 records a prophet’s rebuke for this bargain.

events.title: Kings fall before Omri and Ahab rise
events.summary: A prophet tells Baasha that his house will end like Jeroboam’s. His son Elah is killed while drunk by Zimri, a chariot commander. Zimri rules seven days and burns the palace over himself. Omri defeats a rival and becomes king. He buys the hill of Samaria and builds his capital there. His son Ahab marries Jezebel of Sidon and builds a temple for Baal. Ahab does more evil than all before him. In his days a man rebuilds Jericho at the cost of two sons.
events.detail: This chapter moves through five rulers in thirty-four verses. Three of them die by violence or fire. Verse 24 records the one act of Omri that lasts. He buys a hill at a fair price and names the city for its seller. Samaria remains the capital until the kingdom falls (2 Kings 17:5–6). The book judges Omri only by his worship (verses 25–26). Verse 34 ties Jericho’s rebuilding to Joshua’s curse (Joshua 6:26).

events.title: Elijah and the widow at Zarephath
events.summary: Elijah tells Ahab there will be no dew or rain except at his word. The LORD hides him by a brook, where ravens bring him food. The brook dries up. The LORD sends him to a widow in Zarephath, a town of Sidon. She is gathering sticks to cook a last meal for herself and her son. Elijah asks for a small cake first and promises the flour and oil will last. They do. Later her son dies, Elijah prays, and the boy lives again.
events.detail: Zarephath belongs to Sidon (verse 9), the homeland of Jezebel (16:31). The prophet is sent outside Israel to be fed. His host is a widow with one handful of meal (verse 12). She speaks of “the LORD your God,” not her own. Elijah asks her to feed him first and gives a promise (verses 13–14). Verse 15 says she went and did it. Jesus later cites her in Luke 4:25–26.

events.title: Elijah confronts Ahab at Carmel
events.summary: In the third year of drought the LORD sends Elijah to Ahab. Ahab’s steward Obadiah has hidden a hundred prophets from Jezebel. Elijah gathers Israel and four hundred fifty prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel. Each side prepares a bull, and the God who answers by fire is God. Baal’s prophets cry out all day, and nothing happens. Elijah rebuilds the LORD’s altar and drenches it with water. He prays, and fire falls and burns up everything. The people confess the LORD, Baal’s prophets are killed, and rain comes.
events.detail: Elijah’s question in verse 21 allows no middle position. The people say nothing, since they have been keeping both. He then sets terms that favor the other side. Baal’s prophets are many, go first, and have most of the day (verses 22–29). Elijah soaks his own offering three times (verses 33–35). His prayer is short and asks that the people may know (verses 36–37). In verse 39 the silent crowd finally answers.

events.title: Elijah receives care and calls Elisha
events.summary: Jezebel swears to kill Elijah, and he runs for his life. In the wilderness he sits under a tree and asks to die. An angel twice wakes him and gives him food and water. He travels forty days to Horeb, the mountain of God. There a wind, an earthquake, and a fire pass, and then a quiet voice. Elijah says he alone is left. The LORD sends him to anoint two kings and Elisha. Elisha leaves his oxen and follows him.

words.label: Levites
words.meaning: Members of the tribe of Levi. They cared for the tabernacle and later the temple. The priests came from one Levite family, Aaron’s.

words.label: Ark
words.meaning: A chest or a boat. In Genesis it is Noah’s boat. Later it is the gold-covered chest that held the covenant tablets.

words.label: Covenant
words.meaning: A binding agreement with promises and duties. In the Bible, God makes covenants with people.

words.label: Scribes
words.meaning: People trained to write and to keep records. In the Gospels, scribes also teach the law.

words.label: Assembly
words.meaning: A gathering of people. In the New Testament letters it means a group of believers. Many translations say “church.”

words.label: Tabernacle
words.meaning: The tent sanctuary Israel carried in the wilderness. Exodus 25–40 describes it.

words.label: Baal
words.meaning: A god worshiped by Israel’s neighbors. The prophets condemn Israel for serving him.

words.label: Asherah
words.meaning: A goddess, or a wooden pole set up for her. Deuteronomy 16:21 forbids such poles.

words.label: Cherubim
words.meaning: Winged heavenly beings. Gold figures of them stood over the ark (Exodus 25:18–20).

words.label: Sheol
words.meaning: The Hebrew name for the place of the dead.

words.label: Sackcloth
words.meaning: Rough cloth worn to show grief or repentance.

words.label: Firstborn
words.meaning: The oldest child. A firstborn son received a double share of the inheritance (Deuteronomy 21:17).

words.label: Redeem
words.meaning: To buy back a person or property. The word is also used for God’s rescue of people.

words.label: Anoint
words.meaning: To pour oil on a person or thing to set it apart. Kings and priests were anointed.

words.label: Remnant
words.meaning: The part of a people that survives a disaster.

words.label: Zion
words.meaning: A hill in Jerusalem. The name is also used for the city and its people.

words.label: Concubine
words.meaning: A woman joined to a man’s household with lower standing than a wife.

words.label: Bondservant
words.meaning: A slave or bound servant.

words.label: Cubit
words.meaning: A length from the elbow to the fingertip, about 46 centimeters.

words.label: Shekel
words.meaning: A unit of weight, about 10 grams. Silver was weighed in shekels as money.

words.label: Talent
words.meaning: A large unit of weight, about 30 kilograms.

guides.title: 1 Kings: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: A temple depends on skilled workers
steps.text: Verse 14 introduces the craftsman by his parents. His mother was an Israelite widow, and his father a man of Tyre. The verse says he was filled with wisdom, understanding, and skill. Exodus 31:3 uses the same three terms for Bezalel, who built the tabernacle. So the text counts a metalworker’s skill as a kind of wisdom. A man of two peoples makes the temple’s bronze. The bronze stand shown is a regional comparison, not a temple vessel.

steps.title: The divided kingdom begins with a labor complaint
steps.text: The people’s request in verse 4 is an offer, not a revolt. They will serve the new king if he eases the labor. The elders see that the king must first serve them (verse 7). Rehoboam chooses the harsh answer in verse 14. Verse 15 adds that the turn of events came from the LORD. The text names both the king’s folly and God’s purpose. The cry in verse 16 repeats Sheba’s words from 2 Samuel 20:1.

steps.title: An inherited field is more than a commodity
steps.text: Ahab’s offer in verse 2 is fair as a sale. Naboth’s refusal in verse 3 rests on something else. The field is his fathers’ inheritance, and he calls on the LORD. Leviticus 25:23 and Numbers 36:7 keep such land within the family. Ahab sulks (verse 4), and Jezebel asks whether he rules Israel (verse 7). The tablet shows an ordinary field sale, the kind Naboth refuses. She then uses Israel’s own court forms, with two witnesses, to kill (verses 9–10).

chapterMaps.narrative: King David is old and weak. His son Adonijah declares himself king with the support of Joab and the priest Abiathar. He holds a feast and leaves out Solomon and the prophet Nathan. Nathan sends Bathsheba to remind David of his oath about Solomon. Nathan follows her in and confirms her report. David orders Solomon to ride the royal mule to Gihon. Zadok the priest anoints him, and the city shouts. Adonijah’s guests scatter, and he begs Solomon for his life.

Adonijah asks Bathsheba to request David’s last attendant, Abishag, as his wife. Solomon reads this as a claim to the throne and has him killed. He sends the priest Abiathar home to Anathoth. Joab flees to the altar and is killed there. Shimei is confined to Jerusalem and dies when he leaves it. The kingdom is now firmly in Solomon’s hand.

Solomon calls for a sword to divide the child. The true mother gives up her claim, and he returns the child to her.

Judah and Israel are as many as the sand, eating and drinking. The court uses huge amounts of flour, meal, and meat each day. Everyone lives safely under his own vine and fig tree. Hiram agrees and floats the logs down the coast. Solomon pays him each year in wheat and oil. The two kings make a treaty. Solomon drafts thirty thousand Israelites to work in Lebanon in shifts. Thousands more carry loads and cut great stones for the foundation.

chapterMaps.narrative: Solomon begins the temple in the fourth year of his reign. The house is sixty cubits long, twenty wide, and thirty high. Its stones are finished at the quarry, so no iron tool is heard on site. The LORD tells Solomon the promise holds if he keeps the commandments. The inside is lined with cedar and covered with gold. Two gold-covered cherubim stand in the inner room. The walls and doors are carved with palms and flowers. The work takes seven years.

He brings Hiram, a bronze worker, from Tyre. Hiram casts two great pillars named Jachin and Boaz. He makes a huge basin called the sea, set on twelve bronze oxen. He makes ten wheeled stands, basins, pots, and shovels. Solomon adds the gold furnishings and David’s dedicated treasures.

He says heaven itself cannot contain God, much less this house. He asks God to hear prayers made toward it. He names drought, famine, defeat, and exile as times to pray. He asks God to hear the foreigner too. Israel then offers sacrifices and keeps a feast for fourteen days.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD appears to Solomon a second time and accepts the temple. If Solomon walks as David did, his throne will last. If Israel turns to other gods, the land and the house will be lost. Solomon gives Hiram twenty towns in Galilee, and Hiram is not pleased. Solomon uses forced labor to build Jerusalem’s wall, Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer. The remaining Canaanite peoples are made laborers. Israelites serve as soldiers and officers. Solomon builds ships on the Red Sea that bring gold from Ophir.

chapterMaps.narrative: The queen of Sheba hears of Solomon and comes to test him with hard questions. He answers them all. She sees his house, his table, his servants, and his offerings. She says the report she heard was not even half the truth. She blesses the LORD, who made him king to do justice. They exchange rich gifts, and she goes home. Solomon’s yearly gold, his ivory throne, and his golden cups are described. He gathers chariots and buys horses from Egypt.

He builds high places for the gods of Moab and Ammon. The LORD says the kingdom will be torn from his son. One tribe will remain for David’s sake. Enemies rise in Edom and Damascus. The prophet Ahijah tears a new cloak and gives ten pieces to an officer, Jeroboam. Solomon tries to kill Jeroboam, who flees to Egypt until Solomon dies.

The young men tell him to promise a heavier yoke. He follows the young men and threatens scorpions for whips. Ten tribes reject David’s house and make Jeroboam king. A prophet stops Rehoboam from going to war. Jeroboam sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan to keep his people from Jerusalem.

chapterMaps.narrative: A man of God from Judah cries out against Jeroboam’s altar at Bethel. The altar splits, and the king’s hand withers and is healed. The man refuses the king’s meal, as God commanded him. An old prophet of Bethel rides after him. The old man lies and says an angel told him to bring the visitor home. The man of God eats, and a word comes that he will die. A lion kills him on the road and stands beside the body. The old prophet buries him in his own tomb.

He says Jeroboam’s whole house will be cut off for its idols. The child will die when she reaches home. Israel itself will be uprooted and scattered. In Judah, Rehoboam’s people build high places and sacred pillars. Shishak king of Egypt takes the temple’s treasures and Solomon’s gold shields.

chapterMaps.narrative: Abijam rules Judah three years and follows his father’s sins. For David’s sake the LORD keeps a lamp in Jerusalem. Asa rules forty-one years and does what is right. He removes idols and even deposes his grandmother for her idol. Baasha of Israel fortifies Ramah to block Judah. Asa sends temple and palace treasure to Ben Hadad of Syria. Ben Hadad attacks northern Israel, and Baasha withdraws. In Israel, Baasha has killed Nadab and all Jeroboam’s house.

textRoutes.title: Two sons seek David's throne
textRoutes.summary: King David is old and weak. His son Adonijah declares himself king with the support of Joab and the priest Abiathar. He holds a feast and leaves out Solomon and the prophet Nathan. Nathan sends Bathsheba to remind David of his oath about Solomon. Nathan follows her in and confirms her report. David orders Solomon to ride the royal mule to Gihon. Zadok the priest anoints him, and the city shouts. Adonijah’s guests scatter, and he begs Solomon for his life.
textRoutes.detail: Verse 6 says David never questioned Adonijah about his conduct. Verse 18 says the king does not know what is happening. Bathsheba’s words in verse 20 put the decision where it belongs. All Israel is waiting for David to name his heir. She also names the danger to herself and her son (verse 21). Nathan arranges for two voices to bring the same report (verses 13–14). The oath she cites is not recorded earlier in these books.

textRoutes.title: David dies and Solomon consolidates power
textRoutes.summary: David tells Solomon to keep the LORD’s law and to deal with Joab and Shimei. David dies after forty years as king. Adonijah asks Bathsheba to request David’s last attendant, Abishag, as his wife. Solomon reads this as a claim to the throne and has him killed. He sends the priest Abiathar home to Anathoth. Joab flees to the altar and is killed there. Shimei is confined to Jerusalem and dies when he leaves it. The kingdom is now firmly in Solomon’s hand.
textRoutes.detail: Each removal in this chapter comes with a stated reason. Adonijah asked for a woman of the late king’s household (verse 22). Joab had killed two commanders in peacetime (verse 32). Shimei broke his sworn terms (verse 43). In verse 26 Abiathar is spared for his years of loyalty to David. Verse 27 links his removal to the word against Eli’s house. The reader sees justice and advantage served by the same acts.

textRoutes.title: Hiram supplies timber for the temple
textRoutes.summary: King Hiram of Tyre sends greetings to Solomon. Solomon says he will build a house for the LORD’s name. He asks for cedar from Lebanon, cut by skilled Sidonians. Hiram agrees and floats the logs down the coast. Solomon pays him each year in wheat and oil. The two kings make a treaty. Solomon drafts thirty thousand Israelites to work in Lebanon in shifts. Thousands more carry loads and cut great stones for the foundation.
textRoutes.detail: The temple begins with a trade deal and a labor draft. Verse 13 says the draft came “out of all Israel.” Each man spends one month in Lebanon and two at home (verse 14). Verses 15–16 count the carriers, stonecutters, and overseers. Adoniram, who runs the draft, is stoned in 12:18. Chapter 9:22 says Solomon made no Israelite a bondservant. The book keeps both statements.

textRoutes.title: Solomon turns away and adversaries rise
textRoutes.summary: Solomon loves many foreign women and has a thousand wives and concubines. In his old age they turn his heart to other gods. He builds high places for the gods of Moab and Ammon. The LORD says the kingdom will be torn from his son. One tribe will remain for David’s sake. Enemies rise in Edom and Damascus. The prophet Ahijah tears a new cloak and gives ten pieces to an officer, Jeroboam. Solomon tries to kill Jeroboam, who flees to Egypt until Solomon dies.
textRoutes.detail: Ahijah acts out his message before he speaks it. The cloak is new, and he tears it into twelve pieces (verse 30). Ten go to Jeroboam, and one tribe stays with David’s house (verses 31–32). The text does not explain the missing piece. A torn robe also marked Saul’s loss of the kingdom (1 Samuel 15:27–28). The reason given is worship of other gods (verse 33). Jeroboam receives a promise with a condition, as David’s house did (verse 38).

textRoutes.title: Rehoboam rejects the petition and the kingdom divides
textRoutes.summary: Rehoboam goes to Shechem to be made king. Jeroboam and the people ask him to lighten Solomon’s heavy labor. The old advisers tell him to serve the people and speak kindly. The young men tell him to promise a heavier yoke. He follows the young men and threatens scorpions for whips. Ten tribes reject David’s house and make Jeroboam king. A prophet stops Rehoboam from going to war. Jeroboam sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan to keep his people from Jerusalem.
textRoutes.detail: The people’s request in verse 4 is an offer, not a revolt. They will serve the new king if he eases the labor. The elders see that the king must first serve them (verse 7). Rehoboam chooses the harsh answer in verse 14. Verse 15 adds that the turn of events came from the LORD. The text names both the king’s folly and God’s purpose. The cry in verse 16 repeats Sheba’s words from 2 Samuel 20:1.

textRoutes.title: Ahijah speaks and Shishak attacks Jerusalem
textRoutes.summary: Jeroboam’s son falls sick. He sends his wife in disguise to the prophet Ahijah at Shiloh. Ahijah is blind, but the LORD tells him who is coming. He says Jeroboam’s whole house will be cut off for its idols. The child will die when she reaches home. Israel itself will be uprooted and scattered. In Judah, Rehoboam’s people build high places and sacred pillars. Shishak king of Egypt takes the temple’s treasures and Solomon’s gold shields.
textRoutes.detail: Jeroboam sends to the prophet who once promised him a kingdom (verse 2). He hides who is asking. The disguise is useless twice: Ahijah is blind and has been told (verses 4–5). Verse 6 greets her by name at the door. She came for a word about one child and hears about a whole house. The boy dies as her feet cross the threshold (verse 17). Verse 13 calls his burial a kindness, since something good was found in him.

textRoutes.detail: Elijah’s question in verse 21 allows no middle position. The people say nothing, since they have been keeping both. He then sets terms that favor the other side. Baal’s prophets are many, go first, and have most of the day (verses 22–29). Elijah soaks his own offering three times (verses 33–35). His prayer is short and asks that the people may know (verses 36–37). In verse 39 the silent crowd finally answers.

textRoutes.detail: Elijah says twice that he alone is left (verses 10 and 14). The quiet voice between them does not change his words. The LORD’s first answer to his despair was food and sleep (verses 5–7). The second is work: three people to anoint (verses 15–16). Verse 18 then corrects his count with seven thousand. Obadiah’s hundred prophets were also still alive (18:13). In Elisha he is given a successor.

textRoutes.title: Micaiah warns Ahab before the final battle
textRoutes.summary: Jehoshaphat of Judah visits Ahab, who wants to retake Ramoth Gilead. Four hundred prophets promise success. Jehoshaphat asks for one more, and Ahab names Micaiah, whom he hates. textRoutes.detail: The messenger in verse 13 means well. He asks Micaiah to agree with the four hundred. Micaiah answers that he will say what the LORD says (verse 14). Ahab himself knows the first cheerful answer is false (verse 16). He demands the truth and has already said he hates it (verse 8). He jails the man who gives it (verse 27). The disguise fails against an arrow shot “at random” (verse 34).
